name: Plagiarism and AI Detection
title: Plagiarism and AI Detection
answer: Plagiarism and AI detection covers identifying copied text, paraphrased material without attribution, and machine-generated prose in manuscripts, student work, and peer review. It spans traditional text matching against published corpora and newer classifiers that estimate whether a passage was written by a large language model. The work sits inside academic integrity, editorial screening, and research misconduct review. It does not determine intent, only flags similarity or synthetic origin for human judgment.

It spans traditional text matching against published corpora and newer classifiers that estimate whether a passage was written by a large language model. sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: Detection runs on institutional servers, cloud APIs, and local reference databases of journals, books, student papers, and web content. Text-matching systems compare submissions against large indexed corpora and return similarity reports. AI detectors typically run as hosted models that take a passage and output a probability score, often with a minimum character or word count. Many publishers and universities integrate these tools into submission systems or learning management platforms.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Traditional plagiarism detection uses fingerprinting, n-gram matching, and citation parsing to find overlapping strings and near-duplicate passages. AI detection relies on statistical features of generated text, such as perplexity, burstiness, and token probability distributions, often using a classifier trained on human and machine-written samples. Reviewers then examine the flagged passages, the originality report, and the context of citations before deciding whether misconduct occurred. No detector is proof on its own.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk center on false positives, student privacy, and the lack of a reliable ground truth for AI authorship. Submitting a student essay or an unpublished manuscript to a detector can expose confidential work to a third party, and a high AI score can unfairly damage a researcher or student. Institutions increasingly require human review, clear policies on when detection is used, and disclosure of tool limitations. Provenance matters because a detector's training data and version affect its score, and scores should not be treated as evidence of misconduct without corroboration.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The field is moving toward provenance-based approaches, such as watermarking model outputs and recording the editing history of a document, rather than relying only on post hoc statistical detection. Peer review workflows may integrate disclosure of AI assistance and verification of author contributions. As generators improve, detectors will likely become less reliable for short or heavily edited text, pushing practice toward transparent process records and institutional norms. The site's library of research papers and extracted claims will continue to track these shifts.
